title: Strategy by Draft Stage: Early, Middle and Late
brief: What should we prioritize in the early, middle and late parts of our auction: stable PTS, REB and AST early, value in the middle tier, and upside flyers at the end? It must cover how the cost of a mistake shrinks further down the board, when to take safe players versus upside, and when position needs start to matter.
summary: Spend the early part of the auction on proven players who bring points and assists, because a mistake there costs the most and those categories are hard to find later. Look for value among roughly players 51 to 100, buy assists there, and start checking G, F and C slots only once you have about 7 or 8 players. Use your last three or four roster spots on upside flyers, because a safe player at the end of a 144-player draft is no better than what waivers will offer.

sections.heading: Why mistakes cost less further down the board

paragraphs.text: The gaps between draft slots shrink as you go down the board. The gap between player 1 and player 20 is huge. The gap between 50 and 70 is small. In a 12-team league a round is 12 players, so round 3 is roughly players 25 to 36 and round 6 is roughly 61 to 72. Reaching 20 spots in round 3 is bad. Reaching 15 spots in round 6 hardly matters. In auction terms, overpaying for a top-36 player hurts far more than overpaying a little for a player ranked near 70.

Be clear about what counts as a mistake. Buying a player valued around 10th who finishes 15th or 17th is fine. A big miss, like 11th to 30th, does matter. A swing is fine. Paying for a result the player has almost no chance to reach is the mistake to avoid.

Top players are also the most reliable. Over five seasons, about 16 of the 9-cat top 25 repeated the next year. 75% of top 10 players stayed inside the top 25. Every top 25 player who stayed eligible but dropped out still finished top 50. The exact order inside the first round rarely decides a league. Injuries do.

Lower down, ranks are packed tightly. A small drop in one stat can cost a player 10 or more spots. So the gap between rank and expected finish needed to count as value gets wider late. Late in the draft, a small edge is not enough. You need real upside.

sections.heading: Early stage: buy points and assists from proven players

paragraphs.text: Points is the most stable and predictable category. A low-scoring, low-usage player at the top nearly commits you to punting points. Points, assists and FT% are the scarcest categories later in drafts. Big assist players are rare late. So your biggest early bids should go to players with real volume in points and assists. Check each early target: does he add to both, or does he leave you chasing one of them later?

Points alone is not enough. This is 9-cat, so do not pay early for players whose value is mostly scoring. Two-category players leave holes you then have to fix. Players who are elite only in blocks, FG% and rebounds get overdrafted. Do not take them as early as round 3, roughly players 25 to 36. A defense-only, poor-shooting player bought early can leave you far behind in points and threes. The notes do not name rebounds as an early priority. They suggest adding a big man for rebounds later, when your category check shows you need one.

Do not lock into a punt or a planned pair of players. Early, focus on value, and lean into a punt later if one shows up. If a player goes well below his value, take him and adjust the build afterward. Treat the best players available as a group of roughly equal options. If someone else wins your target, move to the next one. Your first four players, and then your first eight, should make sense together. Your 7 or 8 man core matters more than any pair.

Schedule only matters for your top players, roughly your first three rounds. For those players, check games in our playoff weeks 19, 20 and 21, ending 2027-03-28. Avoid having your best player play only two games in a semifinal or final week. Do not worry much about schedule for mid and late players.

sections.heading: Budget across the stages: where the experts differ

paragraphs.text: The experts differ on how hard to pay for the top tier. One side says first-round players among the big names are generally safe, and the data shows top players rarely collapse when healthy. The other side, writing about auctions, says that in a hot room you should wait for bargains and target mid-round value rather than pay full price at the top. To do well in an auction you must be comfortable not owning a first-round player. A workable rule: pay for top players when their prices are fair, and switch to mid-tier value when the room pushes them past it.

Either way, keep some money for the end. If you spend everything early, you cannot compete for late bargains. In the endgame, a team with a few extra dollars can take your 1 USD nominations. Keep long, flexible lists with large groups of late targets so losing one does not matter.

sections.heading: Middle stage: value, assists and positions

paragraphs.text: The best value is usually found between players 51 and 100. There, players can beat their ADP by 10 to 40 spots. In a 12-team league, average is roughly the 75th ranked player. A player close to average in every category can end up around 100th. So in this tier, look for players with a clear strength, not just a flat line.

Assists are scarce in the middle tier. Hybrid guards who give 4 to 6 assists are worth targeting there. Check your category strengths and weaknesses as players come off the board. If you are short, it is fine to pay a little extra to get assists, or to add a big man for rebounds.

Draft for stats and statistical shapes, not positions, until about round 8 or 9. In our league that means about players 85 to 108, when you hold about 7 or 8 players. From then on, check your G, G, G, F, F, F, C slots. Make sure the remaining budget and spots can still fill them, with the three Util slots taking any position.
Do not buy safe, low-upside veterans in the early or middle stages just to win the projected standings. Take them only when they fall well past their value.

Our draft is 144 players, 12 per team, so it is effectively 12 rounds. Several experts say round 10 is already flyer territory, and rounds 10 to 13 are where flyers belong. For us that means roster spots 10 to 12, roughly players 109 to 144. Use at least three of your last four spots on upside flyers. Your last few players should all be flyers. A safe player who only finishes at his slot means nothing.

Define a flyer by his ceiling. Late players should have at least top 70 upside, and ideally top 50. Targets with top-30 upside are worth it even with injury risk. If they miss long stretches, move on. A good flyer could beat his draft spot by 40 to 50 places. Prefer an unproven player with upside over a proven player with a known, limited ceiling. Young players and rookies fit here. Another option is insurance on your star: a teammate who should start if the star misses time.

Safe late players do not help you. Do not take a player at 110 who projects to finish 110th, because that value sits on the waiver wire. A streaming slot is worth about a top 100 player. Late, the downside of most players is just being useless, and most picks from rounds 10 to 13 get dropped and streamed anyway. With daily FAB waivers and 6 adds a week, plan to replace failed flyers quickly.

Once you reach flyer territory, just buy your flyers. Do not try to wait for their ADP. Skip low-ceiling backups when better options are left. For every late player, know the reason: what the upside is, and how likely he is to beat the alternatives.

sections.heading: Safe or upside: read your own roster

paragraphs.text: The choice between safety and upside depends on the team you already have. Players can share a tier on median outcome but have very different ceilings. If you took no risks early, take a flyer later. If you already took several risky swings or injury risks, lean toward steady players with a narrower range.

The experts differ on boring veterans late. One view: they are fine late when they fall past their value, and outside the top 150 they become value picks. The other view: skip low-upside veterans in late rounds, because stable players are worth more only in deeper leagues. Strategy should change with league depth. In a 12-team league, prefer upside for the later picks. For us, everything outside the 144 drafted players is on waivers, so the boring veteran can usually be found there.
